blocks.content: Explore dashboards on Grafana Play to see whether a dashboard stays focused on its question, where a panel's data comes from, what unit its values are measured in, and how a dashboard's controls change the data its panels display.

Open the **Grafana Dashboard**. The dashboard's title, Grafana Dashboard, doesn't say what question it answers. You have to read the panel titles, Memory / CPU, server requests, and logins, to learn that it's about a server's resources and traffic.
Find the **Memory / CPU** panel. The title says what the panel covers, and the values carry a unit, bytes.
Notice the **server requests** panel.

Now focus on the **logins** panel. Both the logins and server requests panels show the server's traffic, and both titles tell you what the graph represents at a glance. Their values on the y-axis are plain numbers with nothing after them. Requests and logins are counts, things you tally, so there's no unit to show.

View the first **Google hits** bar gauge. Here's a vertical bar gauge with five bars labeled A-series to E-series. Nothing says what each bar measures. Its unit is percent on a fixed 0 to 100 range, but hits are a count, not a share of anything. So the label is misleading.

Now, notice the second **Google hits** bar gauge. Here's the same five unnamed bars, this time with no unit, still on a fixed 0 to 100 range. The colors change at 40, 60, 70, and 80. But with no unit, you can't tell what the color changes mean.

Next, look at the **Google hits** gauge. This gauge suggests a value approaching a limit. The limit is 300 with no unit, and the single series is labeled A-series. Nothing on the panel says what 300 hits would mean.
Focus on the third **Google hits** bar gauge. Here's a horizontal bar gauge with six bars named for servers, Backend-ops-01 to Frontend-web-02. The names help, but there is still no unit.

Four panels, one title, no descriptions. You must figure out what each one represents and how they differ.

A focused version would keep **Memory / CPU**, **Memory**, **server requests**, and **logins**, and drop the **Google hits** repeats.
Explore a panel to see where its data comes from: the data source, the query, and the result format.

blocks.title: Find the query and its data source

blocks.content: Open the **SQL Expressions Showcase** dashboard.
Find the **Base Query (A) - Total CPU Usage** panel.
Open the panel for editing.

steps.reftarget: div[data-viz-panel-key='panel-3'] button[data-testid='data-testid Panel menu Base Query (A) - Total CPU Usage']
steps.description: Click here to open the panel menu.
Click Edit to open the panel editor.

blocks.content: Notice the data source for query **A**. It's a Prometheus data source, so Grafana sends this query to Prometheus.
This is the query. A data source holds far more data than one panel needs, and the query returns just the data this visualization needs.

Below the query, the options row shows **Format: Time series**. Format determines how the result is interpreted in the panel, so it must suit the visualization: the Table format, for example, works only in a table. A stat or gauge can still take a time series result by reducing it to one value.
View the display options section on the right of the editor. This is where you configure how the panel displays its data: its title, its visualization, and standard options such as the unit.
Expand **Standard options** if it's collapsed.

blocks.reftarget: [data-testid='data-testid Standard options Unit field property editor']
blocks.content: Under **Standard options**, the panel's **Unit** is set to **core**, the unit its values are measured in.
Explore a dashboard's controls to see how they change the data its panels display.
Open the **Filter variables** dashboard. If Grafana Play asks about unsaved changes even though you changed nothing, select **Discard**.
Find the **HTTP requests** panel. The controls on this dashboard change the data this panel displays.

Focus on the time picker. It shows the time range currently displayed in the dashboard, **Last 6 hours**.

Last 6 hours is a relative time range, which steps back from the current date and time. You can change it to another relative time range, or to an absolute time range between two fixed dates and times.
Notice **Refresh dashboard**. It runs every query on the dashboard and refreshes the visualizations.
View the auto refresh menu. You can select an interval here to refresh the dashboard regularly. Auto refresh is turned off on this dashboard.

blocks.reftarget: input[data-testid='data-testid ad hoc filters combobox filter input']
blocks.content:
Find the **filter** control. A filter narrows the data displayed in a dashboard, and Grafana applies it to all panels on the dashboard.

A filter pairs a label with a value, which is why the control reads **+ label = value**. A label adds context to the data, such as where a measurement was taken.

Variables and filters appear only on a dashboard that includes them. This dashboard includes a filter and no variables.
